title: Pool Position Play: Cue Ball Control Tips for Beginners
description: Learn position play in pool: the four cue ball reactions, why speed matters, and three easy drills to start leaving yourself better shots.
body:
Making the ball is only half of pool. The other half is where the cue ball ends up. Players who run a whole rack are not hitting miracle shots; they are leaving themselves an easy next shot, over and over. That skill is called position play, and beginners can start learning it today.

What is position play?

Position play (also called "shape") means controlling the cue ball after contact so your next shot is simple. Instead of asking only "Can I make this ball?", you also ask "Where do I want to be for the next one?"

Think of it like chess for pool: every shot sets up the one after it.

The four cue ball reactions

Almost every position shot is built from four basic reactions. Learn these first, because the rest of cue ball control grows from them.

  • Stop: hit a ball straight on with a smooth stroke and a bit of draw, and the cue ball stops where the object ball was.
  • Stun: a firm hit with the cue ball sliding rather than rolling. On a straight shot it stops; on an angled shot it slides off sideways instead of rolling forward.
  • Follow: hit above center and the cue ball keeps rolling forward after contact.
  • Draw: hit below center and the cue ball spins back toward you.

Many beginners reach for draw all the time. Draw is fun, but it is harder to control for distance, so it is smart to build a solid stop shot and a gentle follow shot first.

Speed is the secret ingredient

Coaches often say speed matters more than anything else in position play. The same shot hit softly or firmly sends the cue ball to very different places. Before adding fancy spin, practice hitting your normal shots at a steady, repeatable speed.

A simple rule for beginners: use the softest speed that still gets the job done. Less speed means fewer surprises.

Think one shot ahead

Before you shoot, look at the next ball you want. Then ask:

  1. Which side of the next ball is easiest to hit?
  2. Where should the cue ball stop to give me a straightish shot?
  3. Which of the four reactions gets it there?

Even a small improvement helps. Leaving a shot at a gentle angle is much easier than leaving one that is thin or at the far end of the table. If you are still working on making cut shots, our ghost ball aiming guide pairs nicely with this one.

The 30-degree idea (use with care)

You may hear about the "30-degree rule": with a medium-speed rolling cue ball and a half-ball hit, the cue ball tends to leave the object ball at roughly 30 degrees from its original line. It is a handy rough guide, but it is not exact. Tables, cloth, speed and spin all change the result, so treat it as a starting point and test it on your own table.

Three drills to try this week

1. The long stop shot

Put the cue ball on the head spot and an object ball on the foot spot. Shoot it straight into a corner with a smooth stroke and try to make the cue ball stop dead. Repeat until you can stop it within a few inches ten times in a row.

2. Follow one diamond

Place an object ball near a pocket, shoot a straight-in shot with a little follow, and try to roll the cue ball just one diamond past the contact point. Then try two diamonds. You are practicing speed control.

3. The "what's next?" rack

Scatter a few balls, then run them in order. After every shot, stop and decide where the cue ball should have gone. If you missed your target, note why: too fast, too slow, or wrong spin?

For more practice ideas, see our 5 solo pool drills.

Common mistakes

  • Hitting everything too hard. More power means less control.
  • Rushing the stroke. Stay down and finish through the ball, especially on draw shots.
  • Ignoring the next shot. Pick your target before you shoot, not after.
  • Expecting a stun shot to stop dead on an angle. It slides off the line.

See position play at the pro level

If you want to watch the best in the world do this under pressure, the Mosconi Cup runs November 27-30 at the Caribe Royale Resort in Orlando, Florida, with Team Europe facing Team USA. In the US, ESPN holds the rights, and matches stream on ESPN+ and WNT TV. Watch how often the pros leave themselves a perfect next shot; it looks effortless because of the speed control above. Follow all the action on our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub, find more events on the pro events calendar, and browse more how-tos in our guides.

The takeaway

Start with a good stop shot, add gentle follow, keep your speed soft and think one ball ahead. Do that and you will be running more balls long before you master any fancy spin.
